interest: State refused Japan's bid to station naval oil inspectors in Los Angeles; Japan then tried Mexico.
keywords: Agents of Japan in the United States
overview: This file comprises official records of the U.S. Department of State from decimal file 894.01B11, titled 'Agents of Japan in the United States', spanning January 1940 through April 1941. The primary portion of the file (pages 1–14) consists of consecutive administrative docket sheets ('List of Papers', Sheets 36 to 49) recording diplomatic communications between the Japanese Embassy, the Department of State, the Treasury Department, the Department of Justice, and the War and Navy Departments concerning Japanese government agents, military and naval inspectors, technical experts, and students in the United States. These docket entries focus heavily on diplomatic requests for federal income tax exemptions under Section 116(h) of the Internal Revenue Code and the facilitation of sailing permits for departing personnel, while also documenting U.S. vigilance over Japanese intelligence activities, language officers, and Japan's attempts to expand naval fuel inspection personnel in Los Angeles to oversee strategic oil purchases. The file concludes (page 15) with an internal memorandum prepared by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on April 19, 1941, summarizing a dispatch from the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo regarding Japan's 1941–1942 national budget, wartime appropriations, bond issuances, and domestic economic conditions.

subfiles.about: Cumulative docket sheets registering incoming and outgoing communications and diplomatic notes regarding Japanese government agents and personnel in the United States from January 1940 to March 1941.
keywords: Agents of Japan in the United States
subfiles.summary: This fourteen-page docket register (Sheets 36 to 49 of State Department decimal file 894.01B11) records diplomatic correspondence between the Japanese Embassy, the Department of State, the Treasury Department, the Department of Justice, and the War and Navy Departments. The predominant subject is reciprocal federal income tax exemption under Section 116(h) of the Internal Revenue Code for Japanese naval and military inspectors, technical experts, students, and exposition officials, along with clearances for sailing permits upon departure. The entries also reflect U.S. surveillance of Japanese activities, documenting the State Department's rejection of Japan's proposal to expand its Naval Inspector's Office to Los Angeles for oil purchasing, intelligence regarding a covert oil inspection office in Mexico, and inquiries into the diplomatic status of Japanese military language officers.
subfiles.title: State Department List of Papers: File 894.01B11, Agents of Japan in the United States (Sheets 36–49)
